📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that director Louis HotHotHot is living up to his name. His feature documentary The Year of the Ghost won Best Film in International Competition Thursday as the 39th International Documentary Festival Amsterdam presented its awards.

The Chinese-born filmmaker, also known as Louis Liu, also won Best Editing in International Competition, sharing that prize with his co-editor Chris van Oers.

The IDFA program indicates in The Year of the Ghost, HotHotHot “fearlessly turns his camera on his own family… Using archival footage, animation, and unflinchingly candid conversations, Louis HotHotHot explores how modern Chinese history and misogyny affect the lives of women. This intimate family portrait unfolds into a compelling story about the status of women and changing family culture in China.” Related Stories Documentary IDFA Confirms Winning Projects In Forum Section, With Prizes Worth More Than €30,000 Documentary 'NAZA' Team Sticking To Plan To Release Shattering Documentary On The Guardian Website Within Weeks -- IDFA.

The award for Best Film in International Competition comes with a €15,000 cash prize. Watch on Deadline.

It has been revealed that “The jury was astonished by this work of singular artistic vision exploring deep family dynamics and connections, set against the wider societal forces and gender constraints inherited across generations,” wrote jury members Barbara Orlicz-Szczypuła, Hania Mroué, Katy Léna N’diaye, Oscar winner Laura Poitras, and Luuk Bouwman. “Told with bold honesty, a rare attention to detail, cinematic curiosity, and love.”.

Separately, The Year of the Ghost won Best Dutch Film, earning a €5,000 prize.

The Special Mention for International Competition went to Hazara Town by Khadim Dai. Scroll for the full list of awards.

The IDFA Award for Best Directing (worth €5,000) in the International Competition went to Joël Richmond Mathieu Akafou for Lonan Tché.

The jury wrote, “Through its deeply attaching characters and the subtitle proximity the filmmaker established with them, the film depicts two overgrown kids in their quest for a dream they might never reach, elevating them to almost mythical figures, enduring their human condition.”.

Best Cinematography in the International Competition went to Bardi by Tala Hadid, with cinematography by Tala Hadid.

In the Envision Competition, which IDFA considers to be of equal importance to International Competition, Best Film was awarded to Riccardo Giacconi for Memories of Lightning. That award also comes with a €15,000 cash prize.

According to recent reports, in the feature documentary, “Thirty-year old freelance radio journalist Sibilla travels to a village in Le Marche, central Italy. She plans to make an audio documentary about a shocking event that took place there in 1982, but the village is now little more than a ghost town – earthquakes and an artificial lake have destroyed much of it,” reads the IDFA program description. “Still, she tries to capture memories to create a soundscape of the past with her microphone.”.

Industry observers note that jury members for the Envision Competition included Firouzeh Khosrovani, Hélder Beja, Hicham Khalidi, Isabel Pagliai, and Jonathan Perel. They wrote, “A studio, a village, a hill. A device that renders irrelevant the distinction between what is real and unreal, that exercises precise control over what is noted and what is left unsaid, that stretches time and hunts down stories. A film that captures the silence of things falling, like distant flashes of lightning that are sure to herald the storm.”.

Sibilla Scinti Roger, the protagonist of Memories of Lightning, won the award for Outstanding Artistic Contribution. Best Directing (worth €5,000) in the Envision Competition was awarded to Yuula Benivolski for The Black Box Is Orange.

The Special Mention for Envision Competition went to Memories by Anna Falguères.

all that appears solid is built on blood, directed by Izdihar Afyouni and Gelare Khoshgozaran, won the IDFA Award for Best Short Documentary, which comes with a €5,000 cash prize.

“In a world saturated with images of violence, this short film interrogates what images can hold when representation becomes impossible,” remarked the jury, comprised of Ana Bravo-Pérez, Diana Toucedo, and Yaser Kassab. “Through abstraction, fragmentation, grain, texture, and the material transformation of the film image, documented atrocities are displaced from their conventional modes of representation. The image becomes matter: a site of rupture, disturbance and resistance, where memory exceeds the limits of visibility and what can be shown.”.

A Special Mention in the IDFA Competition for Short Documentary went to Six Weeks, 3 Days, and All the Years Before by Ankita Gusain.

Sources indicate that the IDFA DocLab Award for Immersive Non-Fiction went to Michał Stankiewicz for Being in You. The award is accompanied by a €5,000 cash prize.

“The winner proposes a new way of perceiving the relationship between the protagonist and the viewer: a new immersive point of view in which the digital protagonist and the physical viewer melt together into one,” observed jurors Blake Kammerdiener, Natalie Paneng, and Roel Wouters. “Through a tender exploration of life and death, this project invited us to see how VR can be a tool to memorialize while also bringing a sense of embodied presence.”.

The Special Mention for the IDFA DocLab Competition for Immersive Non-Fiction went to Shifting Connections by Tungyen Chou.

Director Ant Hampton won the IDFA DocLab Award for Digital Storytelling with All the Downtime, earning a €5,000 cash prize.

Sources indicate that “Out of visual noise; slowly, you are instructed how to use your fingers to read a performance through a book, synchronizing multiple temporalities,” said jurors Abel Enklaar, Claudix Vanesix, and Pegah Tabassinejad. “This project gently crosses the borders. It exists in between mediums, crafting a slowly escalating waterfall of cinematic moments drifting up from the pages. The work invites us to see the increasing entanglements between technocapitalism, precarious labor conditions, automation of human work, disregards of natural ecosystems, and the upcoming warlords of corporate fascism.”.

The Special Mention for the IDFA DocLab Competition for Digital Storytelling went to Plum Road Tea Dream by Samuel Baidoo.

Along with the Special Mention for International Competition, Hazara Town won two awards: Best First Feature, which comes with a €5,000 prize, and the FIPRESCI Award chosen by international film critics (FIPRESCI jurors included Hrvoje Pukšec, Loeke de Waal, and Paola Casella).

Recent findings suggest that the Beeld & Geluid IDFA ReFrame Award went to The Clearing by Sabine Groenewegen. The award is accompanied by a €5,000 prize.

It has been revealed that the 39th edition of IDFA, the world’s biggest documentary film festival, continues through Sunday. The festival reports admissions of 270,000 to its screenings. The number of professionals attending from around the world was roughly 2,500.

A little piece of Dolly Parton was at the 2026 CMA Awards.

Nearly two months after the country music legend died, her niece Danielle Parton—who was named the brand ambassador of Dolly’s estate last month—wore a dress custom-made for the “Jolene” singer.

In a recent development, the all-white, fringe-forward frock was, of course, covered in rhinestones and included a trim of many colors around the low-cut neckline, bodice and skirt. Danielle, 50, paired the look with diamond jewelry and a pair of gold heeled boots at the CMA Awards Nov. 18.

It has been revealed that “It was made for the ‘Light of Clear Blue Morning’ video that she never got to finish and get to do,” Danielle told E! News in an exclusive interview on the red carpet. “So I'm wearing it tonight in honor of her.”.

And while Dolly’s niece may have been inspired by the “I Will Always Love You” singer’s wardrobe, she quickly found that her aunt Dolly’s words of wisdom have left a far greater impact.

Industry observers note that “Almost immediately right after she passed, I gave myself one day to sit around and cry and feel pitiful about it,” Danielle continued. “Then the following day I had stuff to do, and I remember she'd always say, ‘Well, you just got to get your rear in gear and get to it.’ So that's what I did.”.

But Danielle knows that Dolly’s impact goes far beyond the Parton family.

According to recent reports, “Dolly was such an incredible human,” she said. “I'm a fan of hers as much as I am a family member, and it's always nice, especially as a family member, to see somebody in your own family have a positive impact on other people.”.

As for the tribute to Dolly performed by Vince Gill and CMA host Lainey Wilson during the event, Danielle noted she was “really excited to see those that she's had such an influence on get to pay their respects in their way.”.

With Siri AI now available on both the public and beta versions of tvOS, the new HomePod mini 2 is still waiting for the feature. Apple previously confirmed that Siri AI would arrive in a future software update, but it was not included in last Friday’s HomePod 27.2.1 release, and the manufacturer has yet to announce a rollout date.

Jax Taylor has hit a small roadblock in his recovery from kidney cancer surgery.

Recent findings suggest that the Vanderpump Rules alum's release from the hospital has been delayed due to after experiencing "some complications," a source close to Taylor exclusively told E! News Nov. 19.

"Physically, he’s very sore from the incisions," the source stated, "but mentally, he’s feeling relieved to have the surgery behind him, as it’s something that’s been weighing heavily on him for months.".

Fortunately, Taylor is surrounded by a strong support system, including his girlfriend Lori Krebs.

"Lori has been by his side," the source shared. "The last few months have really taken a toll on him and she’s always been someone who brings him a sense of peace. They’ve been through a lot together and there’s a very deep love and connection between them.".

The insider added, "They’re truly there for one another, and I think going through something like this has only made them realize just how much they mean to each other.".

It has been revealed that taylor, who confirmed his relationship with Krebs earlier this year, had been privately navigating his cancer diagnosis for a while before going public with his health journey. As he shared in a Nov. 19 Instagram post, “This is something I’ve kept private for the past few months because it’s been one of the scariest times of my life.".

Industry observers note that “What I thought was just a kidney stone turned into something I never imagined," the 47-year-old wrote. "My CT scan also highlighted a tumor on my left kidney. After many tests and appointments I found out it was cancer.”.

Ultimately, Taylor underwent a five-hour surgery to have the tumor removed. While the medical crisis put the Valley star in "a really dark place," he credited Krebs for being his guiding light.

Industry observers note that “I honestly don’t know how I would have gotten through everything without my amazing girlfriend by my side,” shared Taylor, who's dad to 5-year-old son Cruz with ex Brittany Cartwright. “She’s been my rock through all of this.".

He added, "She’s not just my partner, she’s my best friend and I feel so insanely lucky to have her in my life.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kristin Hannah’s best-selling historical fiction book The Nightingale will be made into a movie after all.
  • Sources indicate that the project was first sparked before the COVID-19 pandemic, which slowed momentum on the making of the film.
  • For everything we know about The Nightingale movie, read on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kristin Hannah’s best-selling historical fiction book The Nightingale will be made into a movie after all.

Sources indicate that the project was first sparked before the COVID-19 pandemic, which slowed momentum on the making of the film. Now the movie has a theatrical release date set and a growing cast attached to the story.

For everything we know about The Nightingale movie, read on.

When will The Nightingale movie come out?

In a recent development, triStar first set February 12, 2027 as the release date for the film, but then the adaptation was pushed to March 19 so that it has Easter weekend (March 28) to capitalize on. In Feb., the film would have competed with Greta Gerwig’s Narnia film set to release that weekend as well. Watch on Deadline.

Is there a trailer for The Nightingale movie?

In a recent development, yes, a trailer arrived Nov. 19 giving a glimpse of what the Fanning sisters’ French characters will go through in the film.

Who will be in The Nightingale movie?

Sisters Dakota and Elle Fanning, who have been attached to star and produce since the adaptation started gaining traction in 2019, will portray sisters Vianne and Isabelle.

Deadline exclusively reported that Edmund Donovan (Late Fame) landed a starring role alongside the sisters in January 2026. Details of his role are under wraps.

RELATED: TriStar Reignites ‘The Nightingale’ Movie For 2027 Release; ‘To Leslie’s Michael Morris To Direct Fanning Sisters In Adaptation Of Kristin Hannah Novel.

Next to join as first reported by Deadline are Mark Rylance (The BFG, Ready Player One) and Shira Haas (Unorthodox, Captain America: Brave New World).

Deadline broke the news of a quartet of castings that round out the film’s ensemble: Albrecht Schuch, Douglas Hodge, Gwilym Lee and Vinette Robinson.

What is Kristin Hannah’s The Nightingale about?

The story centers sisters Vianne Mauriac and Isabelle Rossignol, who experience German-occupied France during World War II in their own ways. Vianne, the older sister, is more cautious while Isabelle boasts a rebellious spirit. The sisters split up during the war, “resisting in different ways” as Fanning put it when she did Deadline’s Take Ten interview series.

Who else is behind The Nightingale movie?

Michael Morris is directing the film. Dana Stevens (The Woman King) wrote the script for the film. Elizabeth Cantillon will produce for The Cantillon Organization, alongside the Fannings and Brittany Kahan Ward for the Fanning sisters’ production company Lewellen Pictures, and Reese Witherspoon and Lauren Neustadter for Hello Sunshine. The Nightingale was the Reese’s Book Club selection for March 2023. Nicole Brown and Shary Shirazi are overseeing for TriStar Pictures.

RELATED: Albrecht Schuch Joins TriStar Pic ‘The Nightingale’.

TriStar first acquired the film rights in 2015 with Ann Peacock attached to write. Writer-director Michelle MacLaren and co-writer John Sayles were involved in a later iteration, with the Fannings initially boarding to star in a version helmed by Mélanie Laurent from Stevens’ script. At first, the film was set to hit theaters Christmas Day of 2020, and then it shifted a few more times landing on Dec. 22, 2022, but when the Covid pandemic kept delaying the making of the movie, Laurent stepped back to attend to other projects.

Has The Nightingale started production?

Recent findings suggest that yes, Kristin Hannah posted at the end of March that the film had started production. Elle Fanning did press for Margo’s Got Money Troubles in April before the show’s premiere on Apple TV, but she had hinted as had her sister Dakota, that they would start shooting in a few weeks when Deadline spoke with them at SXSW Film Festival 2026.

RELATED: Hello Sunshine’s President Of Film & Television Lauren Neustadter Previews Upcoming TV Highlights ‘Elle’ & ‘Lucky’ And ‘The Nightingale’ Film As Production Gets Underway.

Deadline also interviewed Lauren Neustadter, President of Film and Television at Reese Witherspoon’s Production Organization Hello Sunshine while she was on set in Budapest, where the film is shooting.

iPhone Duo gets one of Face ID’s best features with upcoming iOS 27.3 revision

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (352 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Soon, your alarms, timers, and phone calls will be less disruptive on iPhone Duo.
  • In a recent development, with today’s iOS 27.3 developer beta 2, iPhone Duo gained a upcoming feature: Unlock with Front Camera.
  • Attention Aware features, which were first introduced with iPhone X, check for when you’re looking at the phone before performing certain actions:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Soon, your alarms, timers, and phone calls will be less disruptive on iPhone Duo.

In a recent development, with today’s iOS 27.3 developer beta 2, iPhone Duo gained a upcoming feature: Unlock with Front Camera. This lets you unlock your iPhone Duo in a similar fashion to Face ID, but using the front selfie camera, rather than Face ID’s TrueDepth 3D camera system. But, Face ID is more than just unlocking: it also provides Attention Aware features.

Attention Aware features, which were first introduced with iPhone X, check for when you’re looking at the phone before performing certain actions:.

iPhone will check for attention before dimming the display, expanding a notification when locked, or lowering the volume of some alerts.

Previously, Attention Aware features required Face ID, but iOS 27.3 extends it to iPhone Duo. Like the latest face unlock feature, Attention Aware features only work when using the outer display. However, the face unlock feature does not have to be set up to use the Attention Aware features.

It has been revealed that after updating to iOS 27.3, the features should be automatically enabled. You can enable or disable the feature in Settings → Accessibility → Face Recognition & Attention. You can also enable Haptic on Successful Unlock there, just like an iPhone with Face ID.

In my experience, Attention Aware features will lower the volume of alarms, timers, and incoming calls when your iPhone is already unlocked. It also will prevent the display from dimming and locking while you are actively looking at it. Finally, it will expand and show notification content on the Lock Screen after unlocking with the new face unlock feature.

Angel addressed the crowd in attendance to salute the manufacturer’s durability and make an impassioned case for its mission during a time of cultural transformation.

Sources indicate that “We live in an age of algorithms, and algorithms are very good at what can be measured now. Literature works on another timescale, in a place measurement can’t reach. A machine can now produce the most probable next sentence. Our job is to find, and to keep, the improbable one: the distinctive, idiosyncratic voice with a music of its own,” she mentioned.

Reflecting on the milestone, she added, “Eighty years is a long time in publishing, but not so long in the history of literature. A publishing house, finally, is people standing behind books, for as long as it takes.”.

#51101. 'Ghost Accounts' Are Putting Your Security at Risk, but You Can Protect Yourself

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (484 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

'Ghost Accounts' Are Putting Your Security at Risk, but You Can Protect Yourself

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (484 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that these so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways.
  • Sources indicate that as McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords.
  • In a recent development, you're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that these so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways. That's why it's important to go through the effort to find and delete dormant accounts. Here's how to get started.

Sources indicate that as McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords. While this doesn't mean your information is sure to be compromised, the more places it lives, the more opportunities there are for bad actors to get ahold of it.

In a recent development, you're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years. If that company or service experiences a data breach, not only is your stored data there exposed, but that information (including your password) can be used to access other accounts using tactics like credential stuffing and phishing. This also increases the risk of identity theft, as threat actors can use your name, birth date, and other information to open fraudulent accounts.

Unfortunately, finding and removing forgotten accounts can be tedious. If you have a password manager, the easiest way to start is to audit older items as well as look at security reports that identify weak or reused passwords, as well as data breaches that have impacted your accounts. If you've saved credentials in your browser keychain, go through the same process to find dormant accounts.

In a recent development, next, audit accounts you've created using single sign-on, such as Google, Apple, or Facebook. For Google, this is under Account Settings > Linked apps. For Apple, go to System Settings > [Your Name] > Sign in with Apple on your Mac (or the same path in the Settings app on iOS). On Facebook, this is under Settings & privacy > Apps and websites. Disconnecting these accounts won't automatically delete them, but you can add them to the list to take action. Finally, you can search your email(s) on HaveIBeenPwned and username(s) on IDCrawl or WhatsMyName to find dormant accounts.

Once you've found accounts you no longer use, the next step is to deactivate or delete them, which you may be able to do through the settings or by reaching out to customer support. At the very least, remove all identifying information and change the password, and if possible, patch the address to a burner using your browser's or password manager's hide-my-email feature. If you no longer have access to an old account, that doesn't mean it's been deactivated and your information removed, so you may need to reach out to customer support to find out how to access and delete it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As you get older, a strong core becomes even more notable to help you maintain balance and stability and avoid injury. But the types of core exercises you enjoyed at 20 might not be the types you enjoy today, and for me personally, at 35, I now prefer low-impact, deep core exercises over typical moves like sit-ups, crunches, or planks.

For that reason, I wanted to share one exercise I love for strengthening your core and hips while remaining low-impact for your spine.

One of the best core exercises I use with my dad, who is nearing 73, looks simple but really blasts your core and deep stabilizer muscles. It also strengthens your hip flexors, which are important muscles for walking and running. Read on to learn more.

As a reminder, this exercise is beginner-friendly. Still, if you're pregnant, postpartum, or dealing with an injury, it’s always best to seek personalized advice from an expert who knows you and your body.

I like exercises that keep your spine straight and stable while teaching the various muscles that form your core to maintain and control tension. So, rather than peddling out endless sit-ups, which flex your spine over and over, I recommend trying leg openers.

If you're unsure what "bracing" your core means, I teach you how with a 5-minute bracing routine.

Here’s how to perform leg openers with proper form:.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

A post shared by Tom's Guide Fitness | Workout Tips & Gear (@tomsguidefitness).

Industry observers note that avoid hunching or dumping into your torso. Imagine a piece of string running along your spine and coming out of the crown of your head. Now imagine someone pulling that string to lift you.

Move slowly and with control, using your braced stomach to maintain your upright position. You can slightly lean back, but try not to do so excessively.

According to recent reports, yes, which is why I use it with older clients regularly. The move teaches proper posture and spinal alignment as you keep your shoulders stacked over your hips and avoid hunching or rounding. This also requires your core muscles to activate to hold you upright and keep you stable; a strong, active core protects your lower back.

In a recent development, leg openers also work your hip flexors, which are vital muscles for lifting your knees, allowing you to walk and run. As you abduct the hip, your outer glutes and adductors also switch on; your glutes help stabilize the pelvis, and the adductors run along your inner thighs, sometimes referred to as the groin.

Industry observers note that this exercise is much friendlier for your lower back than moves like sit-ups, as you can support your lower back if needed, and you don't need to use any extreme range of motion, like hyperextension or flexion, or spinal compression. This move also teaches you to control the movement you generate, increasing time under tension, or how long your muscles work, to build endurance.

I like to count four seconds out with a one-second pause and a four-second count back in. If you notice you're leaning back too much, position yourself against a wall to prevent this, as you want to maintain a strong L-shaped position with your body. A soft bend in the working leg is fine if you have tight hamstrings.

#51097. Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2030 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2030 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger.
  • I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.
  • Recent findings suggest that to rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger. The 1843 tale of a miser browbeaten by self-righteous ghosts is (probably) the most filmed story of all time. Dozens of cinematic adaptations of A Christmas Carol have been released in theaters and on TV since Scrooge; or Marley's Ghost came out in 1901. Hundreds or thousands if you count re-imaginings and very special episodes of sitcoms. But which version is the very best?

I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.

Recent findings suggest that to rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you. My criteria for inclusion: It has to be full-length (at least around an hour long); it has to have been released widely, either in theaters, on network television, or through a larger streaming service, and it has to be fairly close to a direct adaptation—modernizations, re-imaginings, sequels, and that episode of The Six Million Dollar Man don’t count (sorry, Scrooged fans). Using those criteria, I’ve winnowed the Carols down to the 17 you see below, ranked from best to worst, along with where you can stream each one.

In a recent development, it's tough to pick a single adaptation of A Christmas Carol as the absolute best of all time, but the 1984 TV movie version starring George C. Scott is unassailable. Other versions do some things better, but this one does everything right—no mistakes. It stays close to the original text; it's perfectly produced; and it has a consistency of tone and vision that makes it the most balanced of all versions of the story. A Christmas Carol might not have the best Scrooge of all time, but George C. Scott's performance is a solid nine out of ten, and this version features the most adorable and pitiable Tiny Tim of all and the best Ghost of Christmas Present, played by Edward Woodward, who played the policeman in The Wicker Man.

Where to stream it: Roku, Tubi, Pluto TV.

Shot in the midst of the Great Depression, the first sound version of A Christmas Carol digs deeper into the despair and horror of the story than any other adaptation. It’s a bleak, German expressionist Christmas flick, and Seymour Hicks’ sickly, haunted portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge fits the tone perfectly. Instead of delighting in his own crapulence, Hicks plays Scrooge like Satan in The Divine Comedy—he's not the ruler of Hell; he's its most tormented prisoner. Scrooge's miserliness is played as pathology. He wears dirty, torn clothing and shivers miserably while eating gruel because he can’t bring himself to burn a single scrap of coal. Even when he converts, it seems like a manic episode instead of Christmas spirit, suggesting this could be a story about an old man going mad.

Where to stream: Sadly, the version on free streaming services like Tubi and Plex is colorized, but you can watch it on YouTube in glorious black and white.

In a recent development, this big-budget musical take on the Yuletide classic turns Dickens up to 11. Scrooge is huge, a raucous, crowd-pleasing musical with hundreds of extras, elaborate sets, and a scenery-chewing central performance from Albert Finney to hold it all together. But Finney and company also manage to keep the emotional core of the story intact. The music is great, with memorable tunes like “I Hate People,” a song that Finney snarls instead of sings. Scrooge has the best ghosts of any version of A Christmas Carol, too—you can't beat the cheesy awesomeness of big-money 1970s special effects.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Pluto TV, Plex.

Before Hallmark devoted its corporate life to forgettable holiday-themed romantic comedies, it co-produced one of the best versions of A Christmas Carol ever made. This entire movie belongs to Patrick Stewart, whose nuanced, layered portrayal of Scrooge is the best that has ever been done. His "conversion" scene is so visceral and honest, it brought a tear to my eyes, even though I've seen the exact scene performed in at least 40 other movies, stage plays, and episodes of 1980s sitcoms. Sadly, the paucity of basic cable budgets in the 1990s results in some chintzy-looking sets and laughable special effects that mar an otherwise top-notch production.

Where to stream it: Digital rental only.

According to recent reports, horror director Ti West's Carol adaptation muddies the moral clarity of Dickens' tale and suggests there's something deeply troubling beneath all the Victorian holiday catharsis. With a few exceptions, Ebenezer hits the familiar beats of A Christmas Carol: It delivers the crowd-pleasing rich-jerk-turns-good story moviegoers expect, but West layers in subtle hints along the way that suggest the floorboards are rotten, and if you dance with Christmas joy too hard, you'll fall into the dark basement below. Ebenezer seems to whisper to audiences, "How much does the conversion of one miserly wretch matter in the face of systemic injustice? And isn't he going to snap out of it when the fright wears off anyway?" Bonus: As you'd probably expect from a Ti West movie, the ghosts are genuinely scary.

Where to watch it: In theaters now.

I'm sticking A Muppet Christmas Carol randomly here on the list because you can't reasonably compare it to other versions of the story. The Muppet version is a thing unto itself. Like the Ol' Dirty Bastard, its style has no father. A Muppet Christmas Carol is absolutely delightful from start to finish, for children, grown-ups, cats, dogs, space aliens, and anything else you got. It shouldn't even work to set Michael Caine's serious portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge against a supporting cast of puppets, but somehow it all seems natural.

According to recent reports, alastair Sim takes Ebenezer Scrooge on a real journey in this movie. In the first act, he plays Scrooge like Capitalism personified, an uncaring, amoral monument to pure acquisition. He seems like a Scrooge who'd scare away ghosts, but when Marley reveals up dragging his trademark chains, Sim is instantly reduced to pop-eyed fear, like the single chink in his armor is the supernatural. Scrooge then regresses to a childlike, bashful figure as ghosts lead him to different visions, finally emerging from his symbolic death to his rebirth as a Christmas-obsessed guy who lives to serve others. This movie might be among the best of the genre, but an unnecessary subplot about Scrooge's business sandbags the movie through part of the second act.

Mr. Magoo's Christmas Carol was the first animated version of A Christmas Carol and the first animated holiday special ever shown on American TV. The main character, Mr. Magoo, was the star of a one-joke, limited-animation cartoon popular in the early 1960s about an old man who couldn’t see very well, so it’s surprising how carefully crafted and effective this version of A Christmas Carol is. It's weirdly meta too: Jim Backus voices Mr. Magoo, who is a (blind) actor performing as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol on Broadway, so the play is bookended with "this guy can't see!" bits. The songs are strange, memorable and funny (listen to "Razzleberry Dressing" above once and you'll never forget it), but the emotional core of the story remains surprisingly powerful. Jim Backus is amazing.

Where to stream it: Peacock, Roku, Tubi.

Sources indicate that I'm breaking my own rule about not including shortened versions of the story because this animated Carol is that great. Its evocative, graceful, hand-drawn look belongs to animation legend Richard Williams and was inspired by the illustrations from the original version of A Christmas Carol. It's a cartoon, but it's not a kiddie cartoon, so the darkness of the ghosts isn't glossed over. Plus, Scrooge is voiced by Alastair Sim, reprising his role from 1951's Scrooge.

It has been revealed that there's nothing wrong with this brightly lit, by-the-numbers take on A Christmas Carol, but it seems designed to appeal to as broad an audience as possible, so the rough edges of the story have been sanded off. The ghosts aren’t that scary. Scrooge isn’t that miserly, etc. It’s fine for a Christmas movie to be lighthearted fun, but the lowered stakes ultimately blunt the emotional resonance of the climax, leading to a mediocre Christmas Carol.

I'm including this version of A Christmas Carol because it's Lifehacker editor Meghan Walbert's favorite. Sorry, Meghan, but this flimsy 1970s TV movie adaptation hasn't aged well. Henry Winkler does a good job as Scrooge, and it's cool to see Burgess Meredith and other old-timey stars, but overall, this is a schmaltzy, plodding film that unwisely replaces a lot of Dickens' best writing with the work of 1970s TV hacks.

Where to stream it: Pluto, Tubi, Amazon Prime.

I really wanted to like Disney’s A Christmas Carol. Robert Zemeckis is a great director and Jim Carrey is a force of nature, but I couldn't get through it. There might be a lot to recommend this version of the story, but using 2009’s technology to create realistic-looking characters was such a puzzling choice. The whole movie looks like a video game cutscene from a PS3 game, and I kept wanting to hit “A” to skip ahead to the gameplay.

Industry observers note that it doesn't seem like the producers of this obscure 2012 straight-to-streaming feature had much money to work with, which is too bad. If they had, they might have been able to better realize some of the intriguing ideas behind this movie. It's a straight-up horror take on the tale, but it just isn't scary. Sadly, you can't carry a feature film on good intentions. Overall, a swing and a miss.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Amazon Prime.

The animation in this 1997 musical cartoon version of A Christmas Carol is dated, pedestrian, and ugly. The songs are forgettable, and Scrooge has a pet bulldog for some reason. (The one good joke is that he named his dog "Debit.") It’s just not good, which is a shame, because the cast is overflowing with talent, including Tim Curry as Scrooge, Ed Asner, and Whoopi Goldberg.

Where to stream it: Roku, Pluto TV, Xumo.

This BBC drama goes for a philosophical, moody version of Scrooge, but it doesn’t come together. It’s dark, grim, and so ponderously self-serious that it collapses under its own weight. In an effort to present aspects of A Christmas Carol that haven't been seen before (like "How Marley got his chains"), A Christmas Carol rewrites the original text from the ground up, but it comes across like Dickens' first draft with a bad case of Surf Dracula.

Where to stream it: Hulu, Disney+.

The current state of Dickens adaptation is not good. Netflix's uninspired, sappy, CGI version of A Christmas Carol tries to tart the story up with slapstick, songs, and jokes, but it’s all cynical, lowest-common-denominator horseshit. The dialogue has been dumbed down and joked up. Scrooge has a silly dog for comic relief. They added scatological humor. Think about this: The minds behind Scrooge: A Christmas Carol read Dickens and concluded, “This story would be better with a wacky dog and fart jokes.”.

A Christmas Carol is such a solid story, even a grade-school production of it can be fun to watch. But a cynical production of it is extra terrible, given the message of the story. This terrible ego project is a bottom-of-the-barrel Christmas Carol because it feels like a money grab. Kelsey Grammer sucks as Scrooge, mugging his way through a lightweight performance. Jason Alexander sucks as Marley. Jennifer Love Hewitt is, well, actually pretty good as Scrooge’s Christmas-past romantic interest. She is a rare bright spot in this dreary movie, however. Everything else is mid to terrible. It’s shot and lit like a TV show; the sets are bland and the songs forgettable. Overall, it has the cynical feeling of assembly-line, “let’s get this shit over with” TV production.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Pluto TV, Plex.

In a recent development, lance Broadway, a former MLB pitcher turned actor who appeared in Marvel’s Agents Of S.H.I.E.L.D., Lucifer and the 2013 film Olympus Has Fallen, among others, has died unexpectedly. He was 43.

Sources indicate that broadway was found dead Tuesday, November 17, in an apartment complex stairwell in Dallas, TX, according to the Dallas County Medical Examiner. The cause of death is pending autopsy results.

In a recent development, broadway made his feature film debut in 2013’s Olympus Has Fallen, the Gerard Butler action film directed by Antoine Fuqua. He portrayed Secret Service Agent O’Neill under President Benjamin Asher (Aaron Eckhart).

Recent findings suggest that broadway went on to appear in several TV series, including Saint George, Kevin From Work, Lucifer, Marvel’s Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D. and Real Husbands of Hollywood. He appeared most recently in two episodes of USA Network’s Colony in 2016-2017.

In 2014, Broadway was cast as Commander Linden in the science fiction thriller Teleios, which was later renamed Beyond the Trek, and released in 2017 as a TV movie by Screen Media Films.

In 2015, he was cast as Devon in the short film Shattered Reflections.

Broadway’s acting career followed a brief stint in Major League Baseball. As a pitcher for the Chicago White Sox and Fresh York Mets from 2007-09, he compiled a 2-2 record with 5.24 ERA. He was signed by the Toronto Blue Jays as a free agent in 2009 but did not appear in a game for the team.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Retailers are churning out early Black Friday deals already, including the likes of Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, and others. If you're waiting around for Friday, Nov. 27 to do all of your shopping, you might miss out on some deals and unnecessarily make the day more stressful than it needs to be. If you're a Sam's Club member, you have access to many early Black Friday deals worth checking out. I spent some time combing through their website and rounded up my favorite tech deals below.

The Bose SoundLink Flex SE is a portable Bluetooth speaker with an IP67 waterproof rating. The speaker even floats in the water, so you can bring it with you into the pool. While it doesn't offer full EQ customization in its companion app, the sound has rich bass depth and clear highs out of the box. It also features a speakerphone, allowing you to take calls and speak with it. It's light and portable, and the Bluetooth 5.3 supports multipoint connectivity and SBC, AAC, and aptX codecs. You can get the Bose 2nd Generation SoundLink Flex SE for $89 (originally $139).

Skullcandy makes fun speakers and headphones, although they're not designed for audiophiles (their sound signature is very bass-heavy). Their Skullcandy Stomp XL Max is their attempt at making a portable party speaker. It comes with two wireless mics, making it a great option for karaoke. It holds 12 hours of battery life (up to 20 hours with certain settings), has an IPX5 water resistance rating, and has LED lights that sync to the music. You can get it for $99 (originally $199).

Getting a soundbar can exponentially improve anyone's entertainment system, but a 5.1 system with rear speakers and a subwoofer takes it to the next level. The Samsung HW-Q65F 5.1 Channel Soundbar is $299 (originally $399), and it's a wireless setup that will keep the harmony of "too many cables" in the house. It supports Dolby Atmos and DTS Virtual:X to give you a 3D audio feel, and it has a dialogue feature that will let you hear the whispers.

Gaming monitors can get expensive swiftly, but you can get decent options on a budget. A great example is the 31.5-inch MSi gaming monitor selling for $129 (originally $179). It has a 250Hz refresh rate and a 1ms response time to make gaming smoother. There's also AMD FreeSync Premium to get rid of tearing and stuttering.

Face unlock is a good compromise for the iPhone Duo – now let’s have it for the Mac

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (854 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When Apple first announced Face ID, the company talked a great deal about how secure the system is, contrasting it to the far less secure image-based facial unlock systems used by the likes of Google and Samsung.
  • Fast-forward to 2026, and Apple is itself now offering that less secure approach as an option on the iPhone Duo – but in a way I consider a sensible balance between convenience and security ….
  • Sources indicate that the first smartphone to offer a face unlock feature was the Galaxy Nexus back in 2011.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Apple first announced Face ID, the company talked a great deal about how secure the system is, contrasting it to the far less secure image-based facial unlock systems used by the likes of Google and Samsung.

Fast-forward to 2026, and Apple is itself now offering that less secure approach as an option on the iPhone Duo – but in a way I consider a sensible balance between convenience and security ….

Sources indicate that the first smartphone to offer a face unlock feature was the Galaxy Nexus back in 2011. This didn’t include any extra hardware, simply using the front-facing camera to take a photo and compare this to a stored image of the user.

It took just days to discover just how insecure this approach is, with unlock achieved simply by holding up a photo of the owner’s face on another device. Yet even as late as 2019, Samsung was continuing to use this approach.

Meantime, in 2017 Apple debuted Face ID in the iPhone X. This has an entire hardware module devoted to it, with infrared emitters and receivers used to create a 3D map of the shape of our face. This cannot be fooled by photos or even models, and Apple noted at the time there was a less than a one in a million chance of it being fooled (with riders for twins, etc).

Industry observers note that face ID projects more than 30,000 invisible IR dots. The IR image and dot pattern are pushed through neural networks to create a mathematical model of your face and send the data to the secure enclave to confirm a match, while adapting to physical changes in appearance over time. All saved facial information is protected by the secure enclave to keep data extremely secure, while all of the processing is done on-device […] The probability that a random person in the population could look at your iPhone or iPad Pro and unlock it using Face ID is less than 1 in 1,000,000.

In a recent development, given the massive contrast in security of the two approaches, it might seem odd that Apple is now adapting a purely visual face unlock feature. The only reason the company is doing this is because the lack of Face ID has been far and away one of the biggest complaints about the iPhone Duo.

According to recent reports, I suspect Apple made the decision reluctantly and over the protests of security engineers. But while face unlock remains a very insecure approach compared to Face ID, Apple’s approach tries to strike a good balance between convenience and security. The following safeguards apply:.

That latter restriction means it can’t be used for Apple Pay, to unlock password-protected apps, to open the Passwords app, or to do anything else that requires authentication – such as changing your passcode or adding a fingerprint to Touch ID.

I do not see any downside provided the feature is off by default and only those who want it will turn it on. Presumably with an explanation of the reasons it gives reduced security.

In a recent development, for myself, I have got so used to using touch ID on my keyboard that I'd likely not make use of it in my business. If anything goes wrong with client information, I want to know, and be able to demonstrate, that I have taken security seriously.

There’s only one other safeguard I’d like to see Apple introduce: geolocking. Personally, I’d want to be able to allow face unlock at home, but disable it when I’m out and about. Currently, the only two ways to temporarily disable it are to toggle it off or to restart the phone. I’d like to see an option to set safe locations, like home and work, with the feature disabled in public.

Given that Face unlock requires only a front-facing camera, there’s absolutely no reason why Apple couldn’t also make it available on the Mac.

Face ID has been something MacBook customers have been wanting for a great many years, and despite a decade’s worth of Apple patents for just this, it still hasn’t happened. Face unlock would be a compromise option that would at least get us some of the way there. I see I’m not the first to suggest this, with Macworld’s Roman Loyola beating me to it.

It has been revealed that what’s your view? If you own an iPhone Duo, will you choose to enable this? If you own a MacBook, would you like the same option on that? Please take our poll and share your thoughts in the comments.

Key Apple memory supplier SK Hynix has warned that RAM and flash memory shortages are likely to last through at least 2030, keeping product prices high. Apple is believed to be one of 14 customers who have locked in priority orders, but the contract does not protect against price increases related to the balance of supply and demand.

Enhancement: Apple is reportedly about to sign a similar contract with Samsung, also permitting market-driven price increases.

SK Hynix says that while AI continues to drive demand and growth, there is little that can be done in the short to medium term to increase supply.

Supply, on the other hand, is not keeping pace with the growth of the market. Given technical difficulty of leading-edge processes and the long lead time required to build fresh production facilities, it expects the structure in which demand exceeds supply to persist through 2030.

The Register reports that SK Hynix has long-term deals with 14 tech giants for priority orders, but these allow for market-based price increases.

Sources indicate that 14 big buyers […] will collectively buy more than half of its output during 2027 and 2028, and some of them want to extend those agreements. The Korean giant doesn’t mind that because the deals include “a mechanism that reflects market conditions within a price range agreed upon with customers”.

In a recent development, apple is used to being in the driving seat when it comes to negotiating with suppliers, but this is not the case where memory and flash storage is concerned. Here, the shortages mean that it will have been forced to agree to contracts that allow significant price hikes in order to obtain guaranteed supplies.

Recent findings suggest that nikkei Asia also reports that printed circuit boards may be the next component to experience constrained supply. Once a humble commodity item, advances in the technology has turned them into specialist tech, with more layers and higher bandwidth requirements. The report indicates “that complexity shrinks the supplier pool and extends lead times.”.

Apple said back in June that the manufacturer was doing its best to mitigate the price increases, but it has so far been unable to do so.

According to recent reports, PREVIOUSLY: Anthropic shares jumped over 30% in the first minutes of trade at their Nasdaq debut before backtracking as the AI pioneer splashed down with the largest ever initial public offering in corporate history. Watch on Deadline.

Sources indicate that the first publicly traded, pure play AI organization priced its hotly anticipated IPO last night at $83 a share, well above the $70 to $78 range initially anticipated, and valuing the company at $1.5 trillion. It opened just before noon Thursday up 30% at about $111, pushing its market value to $2 trillion, before ascending to $115. The stock, listed under the ticker symbol ANT, then skidded to $95 rose, and dipped again. Shares are at the moment changing hands at about $95, still above where the IPO priced, but also well off their highs.

The listing is seen as a litmus test of investor sentiment on the AI sector, which has taken its lumps lately amid heavy spending, a string of outages across sectors, growing public pushback on data centers, safety and jobs, and the ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang from the firm he founded.

In a recent development, the IPO raised more than $107 billion, the largest capital raise at an initial public offering on record, ahead of Elon Musk SpaceX’s $86 billion in June. The base deal covered 825 million Class A shares, some 800 million from the seven co-founders, with a $26 billion private placement layered on top.

Anthropic CEO and co-founder Dario Amodei with top executives and investors rang the opening bell at Nasdaq headquarters in Times Square Thursday with the image beamed onto a jumbotron on the building’s façade. Below, a crowd of onlookers, media and protestors gathered. Signage at the modest #StopTechOligarchs demonstration remarked the IPO endangered workers pension funds and the global economy and noted the company’s own language citing potentially catastrophic risk of AI.

In a note last night, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., called the $83 a share pricing “a clean read on demand: investors wanted exposure to a frontier lab at scale and the pricing reflects it, following SpaceX five months ago as the second core tech stalwart of this cycle to reach the public markets, and we expect OpenAI to follow in 2027.”.

I'm also hoping to see a bigger discount on the Asics Novablast 5 appear at some point, as I prefer it to the Gel-Nimbus line myself as a lighter, livelier daily trainer.

I've recently tested the Saucony Hurricane 26 and it is a big update on the Hurricane 25 thanks to a latest midsole foam, but it's also $80 more expensive right now, and the older shoe is still a great option for new and experienced runners alike.

A security researcher has discovered that some of the world’s most popular websites were compromised in an attempt to steal cryptocurrency from iPhone users.

Industry observers note that A total of 178 websites were affected, including BBC, CNN, HSBC, IKEA, and Zoom. Reasonably recent versions of iOS are safe, and so far it appears that only a few thousand dollars have been stolen ….

Reuters reports that hackers attacked Optimizely, a website optimization platform used by many major websites.

It has been revealed that several of the affected companies said that they have disabled the Optimizely scripts and are investigating potential impacts. Helme notes almost all of the rogue code has now been removed, and that Apple patched iOS after an identical attack method was detected last month.

Industry observers note that the Coruna loader is byte-identical to a sample we analysed in October from a different campaign. The kit’s own comments say iOS 18.7.3 and later, and 26.3 and later, are patched.

Helme monitored the attacker’s wallets and discovered that only $7,040 has been stolen, though it’s not possible to see how many payment card numbers were obtained.

As always, the best protection against this type of attack is to promptly update all your Apple devices to the latest OS versions they support.

#51078. Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1291 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1291 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, you know “the look” by now.
  • It has been revealed that at this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt.
  • Industry observers note that to borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, you know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font. But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”.

It has been revealed that at this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “thinking models”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

Industry observers note that to borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

Industry observers note that the problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

For example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

Those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT showed me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

While most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”.

The reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

Sources indicate that this pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic.".

In a recent development, if there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

In a recent development, one of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text.

It has been revealed that in every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

According to recent reports, the generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model, so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

This is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

To a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

That means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As Netflix‘s The Body surpasses 5M views in its first week, a petition to remove the show from the platform is also growing in numbers.

Criticizing the “blasphemous anti-Christian series” from creator Quinn Shephard ahead of its release last week, the CitizenGo petition has accumulated more than 126K signatures calling on Netflix to “stop defiling the faith of millions of Christian families and cancel The Body before it reaches our living rooms.” Deadline has reached out to Netflix.

“Once the show reaches your living room and your teenager’s phone, the damage is done. Nobody can take it back,” reads the petition addressed to Netflix’s Chief Content Officer Peter Rice.

It seems the alleged damage might already have been inflicted, with Netflix reporting that the coming-of-age horror series received 5.1M views in its first five days, landing at No. 3 on the streamer’s Global Top 10 English TV list, in addition to ranking in the Top 10 in 80 countries. Watch on Deadline.

The petition takes concern with the depiction of “Christian schoolgirls, a dark initiation ritual, the Devil and ‘prophetic visions'” in the show’s trailer.

In a recent development, “This is a pattern. First Netflix mocked Jesus Christ Himself in The First Temptation of Christ. Then it sexualized eleven-year-old girls in Cuties. Now it has come for Christian schoolgirls,” it reads. “Each time, Netflix pushes one step further into the family home.

According to recent reports, shephard, whose grandmother was an Evangelical minister, previously told Deadline, “We weren’t trying to make a show that was hyper-critical of religion. Obviously, religion is a theme in the show, and it touches on it in a lot of ways.”.

‘The Hunger Games’ Is About Oppression and Sacrifice. Why Does Hollywood Market It With Luxury?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1200 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollingstone

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in author Suzanne Collins’ dystopian YA novel The Hunger Games, a reluctant teen revolutionary named Katniss Everdeen destroys a fascist government that broadcasts children fighting to the death for sport.
  • In a recent development, in the close to two decades since Collins published The Hunger Games in 2008, the now five-novel series has grown into a cultural phenomenon with 100 million books sold and a blockbuster film franchise.
  • In Sunrise on the Reaping, Haymitch is chosen as one of District 12’s male tributes — sent with Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), Wyatt Callow (Ben Wang), and Louella McCoy (Molly McCann) to the Capitol to fight to the death in a deceptively pastoral arena.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in author Suzanne Collins’ dystopian YA novel The Hunger Games, a reluctant teen revolutionary named Katniss Everdeen destroys a fascist government that broadcasts children fighting to the death for sport. The book makes pointed critiques of the fictional Capitol’s ruling class, constantly juxtaposing government-created poverty, violence, and forced labor with a cadre of one percenters whose lives are focused on high fashion, merriment, and excess. It’s a moral lesson served on a platter for middle-grade readers: Look for the bad guys — they’re the ones in the sparkling ball gowns, fat and happy while the protagonists suffer.

In a recent development, in the close to two decades since Collins published The Hunger Games in 2008, the now five-novel series has grown into a cultural phenomenon with 100 million books sold and a blockbuster film franchise. Out Nov. 20, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, based on the 2025 book of the same name, is the latest adaptation of Collins’ world to the screen — a prequel charting the heartbreaking life of Haymitch Abernathy before he was Katniss’ drunk mentor and friend. (Joseph Zada stars in Sunrise on the Reaping; in the original films, an older Haymitch is played by Woody Harrelson.) With newly introduced stars and the return of original cast members Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, and Harrelson, Sunrise on the Reaping has been positioned as the dominant big-budget film of the Thanksgiving holiday, enjoying months of promotional stunts, lavish influencer parties, international installations, and couture-themed red carpets. It’s a blitz of glossy promotion for the sixth film in the franchise and the second in under three years. So why is it, after all this time, The Hunger Games franchise still hasn’t figured out that its marketing misses the entire point of its films?

In Sunrise on the Reaping, Haymitch is chosen as one of District 12’s male tributes — sent with Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), Wyatt Callow (Ben Wang), and Louella McCoy (Molly McCann) to the Capitol to fight to the death in a deceptively pastoral arena. But while citizens of Panem revel in the mental games of sponsors, allies, and grievous bloodshed, Haymitch is drafted to be the linchpin of a secret District rebellion. If Katniss is a symbol later in the series, Haymitch is a blunt weapon in his standalone film — a devastating and tragic example that revolution often requires sacrifices from people who will never see the fruits of their labor. But you wouldn’t be able to tell that from Sunrise on the Reaping’s pre-release campaign. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century.

Sources indicate that for Paris’ October Fashion Week, the studio behind the film, Lionsgate, held a Sunrise on the Reaping-themed costume exhibition at the sculpture garden of the Musée Rodin, a two-day experience titled “Elegance Is Authority: The Story, Style and Power of Panem.” Cast from the film attended the opening, complete with a six-course dinner incorporating themes for each of the 12 Districts, according to WWD. Outside the film’s promotional bubble, social media timelines were splashed with a viral video of a French orchestra playing the Hunger Games rebellion theme, “The Hanging Tree,” outside during the ongoing French student protests. (They only stopped when they were teargassed by police.) Cosmetics brand Stila was chosen as the official partner for the film and released an accompanying makeup collection, including a “Sunrise Eyes Liqua-Play” shadow collection with shades “Maysilee,” “Lenore Dove,” and “Mags” named after women murdered by the Capitol. At this week’s Latest York premiere, attendees were encouraged to follow a “Make Them Remember You” theme for their attire — advice Haymitch gives to Katniss in the first film in an effort to help her survive. According to Vogue, people dressed in Capitol-inspired party outfits walked over to the official afterparty at the tony Metropolitan Club, which had been decorated with ice sculptures and Panem flags. Everything from television spots to posters, cast interviews, and fan events for the film has had this emphasis on spectacle and excess — a focus that completely ignores the story’s inherent social critiques. Trending Stories John Mayer Transports Michael J. Fox Back to the Future With Chuck Berry Performance CMA Awards 2026: The Complete Winners List Halestorm, Brothers Osborne, Hardy Sing for Brooks & Dunn at Ferocious 2026 CMA Tribute Stephen Wilson Jr. and Chris Stapleton Collab on ‘I’m a Song’ at 2026 CMA Awards Related Content Hear Ella Langley’s Reflective ‘Hunger Games’ Single ‘Here Then We’re Gone’ New ‘Hunger Games’ Novel Coming in 2025 From Suzanne Collins Where to Stream All the 'Hunger Games' Films Before You Watch 'Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes' 'The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes' Is One Stuffed (But Satisfying) Prequel.

Recent findings suggest that sunrise on the Reaping isn’t the only Hunger Games film that’s fallen into this trap. There’s a consistent pattern of tone-deaf or straight-up ridiculous promotional attempts across the franchise. In 2025, Lionsgate unveiled a Hunger Games merch collaboration with fast-fashion organization Shein — which fans balked at, considering the books’ themes about child exploitation and labor rights stand in opposition to the clothing giant known for its brutal working conditions. In 2014, for Mockingjay — Part 1, the Hunger Games promotional team released a version of “The Hanging Tree” titled the “Rebel Remix” — EDM tones and synth added to make the dirge fit for radio play. “Are you, are you/Coming to the tree?” a sped-up version of Lawrence’s voice sings, calling for rebels to fight the Capitol and “Wear a necklace of hope/Side by side with me.” (Yeah, seems fun to dance to.) Perhaps the most notorious example happened in 2013, when makeup brand CoverGirl debuted its Capitol Collection, inspired by the best and richest looks in Panem. The backlash was so immediate that it inspired one the most longstanding memes on Tumblr — a parody Katniss Everdeen makeup tutorial with the instructions “we’re going to use a black eyeshadow to represent the coal mines that her father was smashed to death in.”.

It has been revealed that when Collins published A Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes in 2020, her first Hunger Games book in a decade, she told her publisher she had returned to the story because she thought people were beginning to “lose sight” of the dangers of authoritarian rule and what it takes to slowly dismantle a democracy. It’s not a coincidence that younger generations are flocking back to dystopian stories — the ones publishers and studios alike were convinced were flagging — at the same time that they’re becoming more politically minded. Collins’ books and the films based on them present a fictionalized and desperate endpoint to totalitarian ideas; one that readers and moviegoers are treating as more vital than ever. But in the promotion of these films, Hollywood not only misrepresents the message of its source material, but betrays a striking lack of faith in the rich world the series has built — and the viewers who believe in its power.

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (892 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

💡 Key Takeaways
  • First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings.
  • According to recent reports, you can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers.
  • Would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

According to recent reports, you can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

Would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

In the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.).

Sources indicate that in the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

Here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart quickly led to women posting the waist heart.

Okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

As if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber shows up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?".

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood.".

Nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!
